name: Tryginon

name: Vine Black

name: Ampelitis
what: Earth strongly resembling bitumen; black, dissolves in oil like wax; used in medicines and hair dye

colour: bitumen-like brownish black

name: Exudra
what: Theophilus' dark relief color for faces: red with a little black, drawn round features

name: Proplasmos

name: Glykasmos

quote: Put two parts flesh pigment and one part (or less) undercoat pigment in a shell, then mix

name: Sarka
what: Byzantine flesh pigment (sarka): white, ochre and cinnabar

quote: [T]ake white, a little ocher, and cinnabar in a moderate amount ... reddish white rather than yellow
colour: reddish white with ochre: light warm pink-tan

name: Membrina
what: Theophilus' basic color for faces and bodies: burnt (yellowed) ceruse mixed with white ceruse and cinnabar

name: Lumina
what: Theophilus' highlight: ground ceruse mixed with the simple flesh color
citation: Theophilus, De diversis artibus 1.5 (tr. Hendrie, 1847)
quote: misce cum simplici membrina cerosam tritam, et compone colorem, qui dicitur lumina
colour: Membrina lightened with lead white

name: Veneda
what: Theophilus' grey for the pupils: black mixed with a little white (lime on walls)
citation: Theophilus, De diversis artibus 1.6 (tr. Hendrie, 1847), with Hendrie’s note on Veneda
quote: mix black with a little white, which colour is called veneda / Veneda, a grey colour
colour: neutral mid grey

name: Prasinus
what: Theophilus' prasinus: a preparation 'having the appearance of a green color with black', dissolved in water, used on new walls
citation: Theophilus, De diversis artibus 1.2 (tr. Hendrie, 1847)

name: Succus

citation: Theophilus, De diversis artibus 1.14 (tr. Hendrie, 1847), with Hendrie’s note on Succus

colour: sap-green: dark yellowish olive

name: Manisc
what: Theophilus' manisc (menesch), a violet ground for draperies, shaded with folium and lit with lazur

quote: Mix manisc with folium ... / a violet colour would coincide with the directions for the use of manisc
colour: Hendrie reads it as violet: muted blue-violet

name: Folium
what: Plant color of three kinds (red, purple, blue) used for books and draperies; here the purple
citation: Theophilus, De diversis artibus 1.35 (tr. Hendrie, 1847)
quote: There are three kinds of folium, one red, another purple, a third blue
colour: purple kind: mid red-purple

name: Lazur
what: Theophilus' blue for draperies, lightened with white; Hendrie takes it for the deep-blue lapis armenus
citation: Theophilus, De diversis artibus 1.14 (tr. Hendrie, 1847), with Hendrie’s note on Lazur
quote: with pure lazur lighten above this ... / the deep blue lapis armenus
colour: deep blue (navy 0E1638/041B52 region)

name: Spanish Green
what: Copper green made by pouring warm vinegar on scraped copper plates
citation: Theophilus, De diversis artibus 1.38 (tr. Hendrie, 1847)

colour: verdigris-type copper acetate: blue-green; moved from the blue-green 3B8C7A to the green Theophilus names

name: Salt Green

colour: copper chloride-type green: yellower than Spanish green

name: Tin Leaf
what: Polished tin foil laid on wood under oil colors for 'transparent' pictures
citation: Theophilus, De diversis artibus 1.29 (tr. Hendrie, 1847)

name: Cerussa Usta

name: Sinopis

colour: red ochre, mid dull red (bundled A43820)

name: Cicerculum
what: The African sinopis, sold cheaply

name: Rubrica
what: Red earth (red ochre); Egyptian and African kinds used for wood and painting
citation: Pliny, Natural History 35.14-15

colour: dull brownish red (bundled 833923)

name: Miltos
what: The Greek name for red earth, with which Homer's ships were colored
citation: Pliny, Natural History 33.38
quote: The Greeks call this red earth "miltos,"
colour: red ochre

name: Lemnian Earth
what: Rubrica of Lemnos, sold in sealed packages ('sphragis'); used as an undercoat for minium
citation: Pliny, Natural History 35.14
quote: looking upon earth of Lemnos as a rubrica of the highest quality. This last approaches very nearly to minium
colour: brighter red earth, toward minium

name: Red Ochre
what: Iron-oxide red earth; best from Sinope, Egypt, the Balearics and Lemnos; on the lips and beads of a Fayum portrait
citation: Vitruvius, De architectura 7.7.2 (tr. Gwilt); ColourLex: a Fayum portrait of a woman (National Gallery of Art), after Delaney et al., Scientific Reports 7 (2017)

what: Iron oxide; one of the iron earths behind nearly every tone in Tebtunis and Fayum portraits

quote: including hematite, goethite, jarosite / natural minerals: natrojarosite, goethite, hematite
colour: ground hematite: deep purplish brown-red

name: Usta
what: Burnt ceruse (or calcined marbled sil quenched in vinegar); first used by Nicias; 'without usta shadows cannot be made'
citation: Pliny, Natural History 35.20

colour: Pliny names the best kind 'purpurea'; read as a deep dull red for shadow

name: Sandyx
what: Sandarach calcined with an equal part of rubrica; Davy thought it approached crimson
citation: Pliny, Natural History 35.23

colour: red lead + red earth: strong warm red

name: Syricum

citation: Pliny, Natural History 35.24
quote: It is prepared from a combination of sinopis with sandyx
colour: between Sinopis and Sandyx

name: Bole
what: Reddish clay; Byzantine painters used it with umber to draw features and to redden ochre for flesh
citation: Dionysios of Fourna, Hermeneia §17, 19 (tr. Parpulov, Dolgikh and Cowe, Dumbarton Oaks Papers 64, 2010)
quote: [one] dram of umber, [one] dram of bole / If you lack yellow-red ocher, add a little bole to another ocher
colour: red-brown clay

name: Cinnabaris
what: Cinnabar (mercury sulphide) from Sisapo in Spain, refined at Rome; used by the ancients for monochrome pictures
citation: Pliny, Natural History 33.39-40
quote: The ancients used to paint with cinnabaris those pictures of one colour
colour: mineral cinnabar: deep slightly bluish red

name: Red Lead

name: Sandarach

colour: Pliny: flame colour, orange

name: Orpiment
what: Yellow arsenic sulphide (Greek arsenikon), best from Pontus; much used by painters
citation: Vitruvius, De architectura 7.7.5 (tr. Gwilt); Pliny, Natural History 33.22

colour: golden yellow per ColourLex orpiment swatch

name: Sil
what: Yellow ochre found in gold and silver mines; Attic, marbled, Scyric, Achaian, Gallic kinds
citation: Pliny, Natural History 33.56

colour: yellow ochre

name: Attic Sil
what: The best sil, used by Polygnotus and Micon and later for strong lights; Apelles' yellow
citation: Pliny, Natural History 33.56, 35.32

colour: light bright ochre for highlights

name: Scyric Sil
what: Compressed sil from Scyros, used with the Lydian kind for shadow painting
citation: Pliny, Natural History 33.56
quote: the compressed sil, known to some persons as Scyric sil ... employed the Scyric and Lydian kinds for shadow painting
colour: shadow ochre: mid brown (bundled 8D603E)

name: Yellow Ochre
what: Hydrated iron-oxide earth; on the yellow beads and background of a Fayum portrait
citation: ColourLex; ColourLex: a Fayum portrait of a woman (National Gallery of Art), after Delaney et al., Scientific Reports 7 (2017)
quote: Yellow ochre has been in use since prehistoric times / Yellow beads in the necklace: yellow ochre
colour: ColourLex swatch; moved from C99A48 toward yellow, so it reads as the yellow its name says

name: Attic Ochre
what: Native ochre (Greek ochra) dug in the Attic silver mines, no longer to be had in Vitruvius' time

quote: the best is the Attic sort, which cannot now be procured ... the colour of Attic ochre is produced
colour: pale fine ochre (bundled E7C387)

citation: ColourLex
quote: The pigment had been used since prehistoric times.
colour: ColourLex swatch (bundled C9833F)

what: Iron oxide-hydroxide, the yellow-brown iron earth in Tebtunis and Fayum portraits
citation: Getty APPEAR project: the Tebtunis portraits at the Hearst Museum; Delaney et al., Scientific Reports 7 (2017)
quote: including hematite, goethite, jarosite / natural minerals: natrojarosite, goethite, hematite
colour: yellow-brown ochre mineral powder

name: Jarosite
what: Pale yellow iron sulphate mineral among the iron earths of Tebtunis and Fayum portraits
citation: Getty APPEAR project: the Tebtunis portraits at the Hearst Museum; Delaney et al., Scientific Reports 7 (2017)
quote: including hematite, goethite, jarosite, and a manganese-rich umber
colour: pale greenish-yellow ochre

name: Quaestorian Leaf
what: The second-thickest grade of Roman gold leaf, after the 'leaf of Praeneste'
citation: Pliny, Natural History 33.19
quote: The next in thickness is known as the "quaestorian leaf."
colour: heavier gold, slightly deeper

name: Beeswax
what: Binder of Fayum encaustic and of the red-lead shrouds; the best yellow wax came from Pontus
citation: Getty APPEAR project: the Tebtunis portraits at the Hearst Museum; Pliny, Natural History 21.49

colour: raw yellow wax

name: Punic Wax
what: Yellow wax bleached in the open air and boiled with sea water and nitre; rubbed hot on vermilion walls
citation: Pliny, Natural History 21.49; Vitruvius, De architectura 7.9.3 (tr. Gwilt)
quote: The best wax is that known as Punic wax ... yellow wax is first blanched in the open air
colour: bleached wax: creamy off-white

name: Lead White
what: Basic lead carbonate made with lead and vinegar; in the flesh tones of Fayum portraits
citation: ColourLex; ColourLex: a Fayum portrait of a woman (National Gallery of Art), after Delaney et al., Scientific Reports 7 (2017)
quote: Lead white has been in use since antiquity / Flesh tones: ochres, lead white
colour: warm white per ColourLex swatch

name: Melinum
what: White earth from Melos; Apelles' white
citation: Pliny, Natural History 35.19, 35.32
quote: Melinum, too, is a white colour, the best being the produce of the Isle of Melos
colour: earthy white, slightly warm

name: Paraetonium
what: White from Paraetonium in Egypt, said to be sea-foam with slime; the most unctuous white
citation: Pliny, Natural History 35.18
quote: This is the most unctuous of all the white colours
colour: clean white

name: Chalk
what: Calcium carbonate, used with madder lake on the tunic of a Fayum portrait and as a base for purpurissum
citation: ColourLex, calcite; ColourLex: a Fayum portrait of a woman (National Gallery of Art), after Delaney et al., Scientific Reports 7 (2017)
quote: Chalk and the other forms of calcium carbonate have been in use since antiquity / Red tunic: madder lake and chalk
colour: neutral white

name: Gypsum
what: Calcium sulphate; white ground for panels and the sketches on Tebtunis portraits
citation: Getty APPEAR project: the Tebtunis portraits at the Hearst Museum; Theophilus, De diversis artibus 1.19 (tr. Hendrie, 1847)
quote: these portraits are unique in the APPEAR corpus, as they have gypsum / take gypsum, burnt like lime, or chalk
colour: bright white

name: Cimolian Earth
what: Cretaceous earth used in medicine and for scouring cloth; one kind white, one tinged like purpurissum

quote: two kinds of Cimolian earth, employed in medicine, the one white and the other inclining to the tint of purpurissum
colour: greyish clay white (bundled D6D0C8)

name: Argentaria
what: 'Silver chalk', named for the brightness it gives silver; dyed with purple to make purpurissum
citation: Pliny, Natural History 35.58, 35.26
quote: There is another cretaceous earth, known as "argentaria," from the brightness which it imparts to silver
colour: chalk white, slightly grey

name: Green Earth
what: Greyish green clay earth, in use from antiquity; base of Byzantine flesh undercoats
citation: ColourLex
quote: Green earth has been in use since antiquity times until the present day.
colour: ColourLex swatch: muted grey-olive green

name: Theodotion
what: Green chalk; the best from Smyrna, named after Theodotus, on whose land it was found
citation: Vitruvius, De architectura 7.7.2 (tr. Gwilt)
quote: Green chalk is also found in many places; but the best comes from Smyrna, and is called by the Greeks theodotion
colour: green earth/chalk, paler than Green Earth

name: Appianum
what: Cheap green made from a green chalk, imitating chrysocolla
citation: Pliny, Natural History 35.29
quote: the green known as "appianum," a fair imitation of chrysocolla ... prepared from a green chalk
colour: green chalk, light yellow-green grey

name: Chrysocolla
what: Copper green found in mines, dyed with the plant lutum; best when it has 'the tint of corn when in a state of the freshest verdure'

name: Verdigris
what: Copper acetate made by hanging copper over vinegar; in the green beads of a Fayum portrait (in beeswax)

name: Malachite
what: Green copper carbonate mineral, used in ancient Egypt

quote: Malachite has been used in ancient Egypt
colour: ColourLex swatch

name: Egyptian Blue
what: Synthetic copper calcium silicate made from sand, natron and copper; in Fayum portrait backgrounds

quote: Blue was first manufactured at Alexandria ... Egyptian blue appears only in the neutral background color

name: Armenium
what: Blue mineral from Armenia (azurite), like caeruleum but whiter

quote: the colour being pretty much that of caeruleum ... It differs from caeruleum in a certain degree of whiteness

name: Azurite
what: Blue copper carbonate mineral, in use since antiquity
citation: ColourLex
quote: Azurite has been in use since antiquity until about the beginning of the 18th century.
colour: ColourLex swatch, deep blue

name: Indicum
what: Indigo from India: black as a powder, purple and blue when diluted; used in Tebtunis portraits

colour: indigo: blackish navy (bundled 0E1638)

name: Purpurissum
what: Silver chalk dyed with purple in the dyer's cauldron; best from Puteoli

quote: argentaria or silver chalk is dyed along with purple cloth
colour: chalk dyed purple: mid pinkish purple

name: Ostrum
what: Purple from the marine shell, prepared with honey; varies from brown to violet to red by region

quote: It is called ostrum, because extracted from marine shells

name: Tyrian Purple
what: Shellfish purple; best 'of the color of clotted blood ... blackish to the sight'

quote: It is considered of the best quality when it has exactly the colour of clotted blood, and is of a blackish hue

name: Cartellina
what: The thin glass layer over the metal leaf of a gold or silver tessera; usually transparent and colorless.

name: Stannum
what: Pliny's stannum (tin-lead) used to coat copper vessels so they looked like silver.

what: Colored glass paste cut into tesserae for wall mosaics.

what: Theophilus's 'sapphire' (blue) opaque glass found in ancient mosaic work.
citation: Theophilus, De diversis artibus 2.12 (tr. Hendrie, 1847)

name: Amber Glass
what: Translucent natron glass colored amber by an iron-sulphur chromophore, Hellenistic to early Roman.

name: Natron Glass
what: Soda glass fluxed with natron; most Roman glass is transparent light blue or green from impurities.
citation: Paynter and Jackson, “Mellow yellow: an experiment in amber”, Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports 22 (2018); Fiorentino, Chinni and Vandini, “Ravenna, its mosaics and the contribution of archaeometry”, Journal of Cultural Heritage 46 (2020)

name: Opaque Turquoise
what: Opaque turquoise glass tessera colored with copper, opacified with calcium antimonate.
citation: Fiorentino, Chinni and Vandini, “Ravenna, its mosaics and the contribution of archaeometry”, Journal of Cultural Heritage 46 (2020)
quote: Calcium antimonate was detected in some opaque turquoise and blue tesserae, acting as opacifier

what: White glass tesserae opacified with calcium antimonate or calcium phosphate (Neonian Baptistery, Ravenna).
citation: Fiorentino, Chinni and Vandini, “Ravenna, its mosaics and the contribution of archaeometry”, Journal of Cultural Heritage 46 (2020)
quote: In the white tesserae, either calcium antimonate or calcium phosphate was detected

name: Copper Green
what: Green glass tesserae colored with copper oxide (San Vitale presbytery set).
citation: Fiorentino, Chinni and Vandini, “Ravenna, its mosaics and the contribution of archaeometry”, Journal of Cultural Heritage 46 (2020)

name: Lead Antimonate
what: Opacifier and colorant of opaque yellow glass up to the Roman period.
citation: Di Bella et al., “Lead stannate as component of antique yellow glassy tesserae from Sicilian mosaics”, Mediterranean Archaeology and Archaeometry (2022)

name: Lead Stannate
what: Lead-tin yellow opacifier that replaced lead antimonate in yellow glass from about the 4th century AD.
citation: Di Bella et al., “Lead stannate as component of antique yellow glassy tesserae from Sicilian mosaics”, Mediterranean Archaeology and Archaeometry (2022)
quote: it was replaced by lead stannate from about the 4th century AD up to the end of the Roman period
colour: Median patch of analysed yellow tessera GL10 (Lipari) in Di Bella et al. Fig. 2, rendered at 200 dpi

name: Orange Tessera
what: Opaque orange glass tessera, lead- and tin-rich, from Ravenna's Neonian Baptistery.
citation: Fiorentino, Chinni and Vandini, “Ravenna, its mosaics and the contribution of archaeometry”, Journal of Cultural Heritage 46 (2020)
quote: The higher concentrations of lead (PbO = 20.00 wt%), in addition to the presence of tin
colour: Median patch of an opaque orange tessera (row 2, 6th) in Met 2016.11.1-.50 (obj 708074, Byzantine tesserae, glass/gold/silver leaf) primary image

name: Haematinum
what: Pliny's opaque glass, red all through.
citation: Pliny, Natural History 36.67
quote: there is also a glass that is red all through, and opaque, known as "hæmatinum."
colour: Median patch of Met Roman glass monochrome dish fragment 91.1.1668 (obj 257019; medium just Glass, visibly opaque red)

name: Cuprite
what: Copper(I) oxide in opaque red glass; with copper nanoparticles it gave a Ravenna red tessera its color.
citation: Fiorentino, Chinni and Vandini, “Ravenna, its mosaics and the contribution of archaeometry”, Journal of Cultural Heritage 46 (2020)
quote: its dullish red colour due to the presence of copper nanoparticles and cuprite in the matrix
colour: Median patch of a red tessera (row 3, 2nd) in Met 2016.11.1-.50 (obj 708074, Byzantine tesserae, glass/gold/silver leaf) primary image

name: Sealing-wax Red
what: High-lead opaque red glass colored by Cu2O crystals; it went out of use around the 1st century CE.
citation: Fiorentino, Chinni and Vandini, “Ravenna, its mosaics and the contribution of archaeometry”, Journal of Cultural Heritage 46 (2020)
quote: named “sealing-wax red glass”, is a high-lead glass coloured and opacified by dendritic crystals of Cu2O
colour: Median patch of a bright opaque red tessera (row 1, 2nd) in Met 2016.10.1-.17 (obj 708072, Byzantine tesserae, glass/stone/gold leaf) primary image; not analysed

name: Manganese
what: Manganese oxide colored purple and black-purple tesserae (Ravenna, San Vitale).
citation: Fiorentino, Chinni and Vandini, “Ravenna, its mosaics and the contribution of archaeometry”, Journal of Cultural Heritage 46 (2020)
quote: Black-purple tessera was coloured by manganese oxide
colour: Median of the purple-brown tessera (row 3, 6th) in Met 2016.10.1-.17 (obj 708072, Byzantine tesserae, glass/stone/gold leaf) primary image

name: Terracotta
what: Fired clay; ceramic is one of the materials cut into tesserae.
citation: Getty Conservation Institute and INP, Illustrated Glossary: Technician Training for the Maintenance of In Situ Mosaics (2013), p. 3
quote: tesserae, are obtained by cutting different materials such as stone (often marble or limestone), ceramic or glass
colour: Median patch of the red-slipped Met Roman terracotta plate obj 250093

name: Cocciopesto
what: Pavement of lime mortar mixed with ceramic or stone fragments.
citation: Getty Conservation Institute and INP, Illustrated Glossary: Technician Training for the Maintenance of In Situ Mosaics (2013), p. 18
quote: Pavement made of lime mortar mixed with ceramic or stone fragments without the insertion of other elements.
colour: Median patch of the 'Cocciopesto' photo, Getty glossary p.18, rendered 120 dpi

name: Opus Signinum
what: Lime mortar with ceramic fragments, set with tesserae or stone fragments.
citation: Getty Conservation Institute and INP, Illustrated Glossary: Technician Training for the Maintenance of In Situ Mosaics (2013), p. 16
quote: Pavement made of lime mortar mixed with ceramic fragments into which quadrangular tesserae or small stone fragments are inserted
colour: Median patch (white tesserae largely excluded by median) of the top photo, Getty glossary p.16

name: Opus Figlinum
what: Pavement of rectangular ceramic pieces set on edge in a basket-weave pattern.
citation: Getty Conservation Institute and INP, Illustrated Glossary: Technician Training for the Maintenance of In Situ Mosaics (2013), p. 14
quote: Pavement usually made of same-sized rectangular ceramic fragments, inserted on their smaller side
colour: Median patch of the top photo, Getty glossary p.14

name: Opus Spicatum
what: Pavement of rectangular ceramic elements in a herringbone pattern.
citation: Getty Conservation Institute and INP, Illustrated Glossary: Technician Training for the Maintenance of In Situ Mosaics (2013), p. 15
quote: Pavement made of ceramic elements, usually of the same size and rectangular shape, arranged in a herringbone pattern.
colour: Median patch of the top photo, Getty glossary p.15 (weathered surface)

name: Lime Mortar
what: Mortar of lime and aggregate; the bedding layer that holds the tesserae is very rich in lime.
citation: Getty Conservation Institute and INP, Illustrated Glossary: Technician Training for the Maintenance of In Situ Mosaics (2013), p. 2
quote: Bedding layer - Thin layer of mortar, very rich in lime, applied in small sections over the nucleus.
colour: Median patch of lacuna-fill repair mortar photo, Getty glossary p.19 (a modern repair mortar, not ancient bedding)

name: Mortar Pavement
what: Pavement of lime mortar with stone fragments, without inserted tesserae.
citation: Getty Conservation Institute and INP, Illustrated Glossary: Technician Training for the Maintenance of In Situ Mosaics (2013), p. 18
quote: Mortar pavement with stone fragments
colour: Median patch of the 'Mortar pavement with stone fragments' photo, Getty glossary p.18

name: Pebble
what: Natural pebbles set on edge to make figures or geometric motifs.
citation: Getty Conservation Institute and INP, Illustrated Glossary: Technician Training for the Maintenance of In Situ Mosaics (2013), p. 10
quote: made of natural pebbles of different sizes and placed on their edge, side by side
colour: Median patch of the close-up pebble photo, Getty glossary p.10

name: Faience
what: Egyptian faience, a glazed non-clay ceramic, blue-green.
citation: The Met, Hippopotamus ('William'), Egypt (17.9.1)
quote: Faience
colour: Median patch of a lit area of the glazed body in the Met image of obj 544227

name: Cloisonne Enamel
what: Glass enamel fused into gold cloisons, Byzantine c. 1100.
citation: The Met, Medallion with Christ from an Icon Frame, Byzantine, ca. 1100 (17.190.678)
quote: Gold, silver, and enamel worked in cloisonné
colour: Median patch of the blue enamel of the halo in the Met image of obj 464551

name: Limewood
what: Wooden panel for Roman-Egyptian (Fayum) encaustic portraits.
citation: The Met, Portrait of a thin-faced, bearded man, 160-180 CE (09.181.1)
quote: Encaustic on limewood
colour: Median 60x60 px patches of the unpainted strip at the panel's foot, Met original image of obj 547856

name: Linen
what: Linen wrappings of a Roman-period Egyptian mummy with an inserted panel portrait.
citation: The Met, Mummy with an Inserted Panel Portrait of a Youth, 80-100 CE (11.139)
quote: Mummified human body with linen and mummification material; panel portrait: encaustic on limewood
colour: Median patch of the wrappings in the Met image of obj 547697

name: Shell
what: Mother-of-pearl shell; listed among the materials of San Vitale's Theodora mosaic.
citation: BYZART, University of Bologna: San Vitale, Ravenna, Theodora and her retinue
quote: pâte de verre (glass); gold (metal); mother of pearl; stone (worked rock)
colour: Median patch of Met mother-of-pearl shell adornment obj 327574 (not from San Vitale)

name: Topazos
what: Pliny's topazos, the green gem of Topazos island in the Red Sea (now Zabargad): peridot (gem olivine), yellow-green.
citation: Pliny, Natural History 37.32; GIA, Peridot from Egypt; The Met, peridot ring stone (244991)
quote: Pliny: "Topazos is a stone that is still held in very high estimation for its green tints"; GIA: "In ancient times, peridot crystals were referred to unknowingly as “topaz”"; "Peridot ... is the yellowish green to green gem variety of olivine".
colour: Met 244991 primary image (DP141762), mean of stone pixels (hue 40-120, sat>=0.25) in the 25th-95th brightness percentile band over the clear part of the stone; the dark rim and frosted engraving pull darker (whole-stone median 849035).

name: Pyrochlore
what: Opaque yellow-green mosaic glass: lead antimonate (pyrochlore) crystals in a copper-tinted glass; the most abundant tesserae colors at 6th-c. Hierapolis and in late antique mosaics.
citation: Neri, Morvan, Colomban, Guerra and Prigent, “Late Roman and Byzantine mosaic opaque glass-ceramics tesserae (5th–9th century)”, Ceramics International 42 (2016), fig. 1
quote: "In the most abundant yellow, green-yellow and green tesserae, yellow crystals are dispersed in colourless or green glass with bubbles"; "the yellow, yellow-green, red and orange colours are obtained by addition of pyrochlore and cuprite or metallic copper, respectively."
colour: Neri et al. Fig. 1b (embedded scan, PDF p.19), tessera HA_C_2: mean of the middle brightness half of pixels with sat>=0.3; a second yellow-green tessera in Met 708074 (row 5, 6th) reads A3A446, so the family is A3A446-ADBD6C.

name: Green Tessera
what: Opaque leaf-green glass tessera, Byzantine; greens of this kind were made by dispersing yellow lead antimonate in copper-blue/green glass.
citation: The Met, Mosaic Tesserae, Byzantine (2016.11.1–.50); Neri, Morvan, Colomban, Guerra and Prigent, “Late Roman and Byzantine mosaic opaque glass-ceramics tesserae (5th–9th century)”, Ceramics International 42 (2016)
quote: Neri et al.: "Pyrochlore, once mixed/dispersed in a blue matrix, usually is used to produce the shades of yellow and green".
colour: Median of the inner 60% of tessera row 5, 3rd from left, in Met 708074 primary image (2016_11_1_50_MED_s01.jpg, 4000 px); its neighbour (row 5, 4th) reads 859451. A Roman opaque green stripe in Met 257305 (mosaic glass, late 1st c. BCE) reads 527C34.

name: Luteum
what: Weld (Reseda luteola), "the herb called luteum": the Romans' lightfast yellow dye, also laid over blue to make green.
citation: Vitruvius, De architectura 7.14.2
quote: Vitruvius: "herba quae luteum appellatur caeruleum inficiunt"; Nuruosmaniye: "Weld was already known by the Romans as the best dye plant for a lightfast yellow." Colours obtained: "Olive Green, Yellow, Bright yellow, Khaki".
colour: Estimate from the published colour description (bright, slightly greenish yellow of luteolin on alum-mordanted wool); no measured swatch fetched.

name: Weld Green
what: Vitruvius' cheap substitute for chrysocolla green: caeruleum (Egyptian blue) dyed over with weld, "the most vivid green".
citation: Vitruvius, De architectura 7.14.2 (tr. Gwilt)
quote: Gwilt: "those who cannot afford the use of chrysocolla, mix blue with the herb weld, and thus obtain a brilliant green"; Latin: "et ita utuntur viridissimo colore".
colour: Computed, not observed: multiplicative (glaze) mix of the list's Caeruleum 2E86B0 with Luteum E6D23C; a chalk-lightened ground would sit lighter, toward 557F27.

name: Crocus
what: Saffron (Crocus sativus), the costliest yellow dye and color of antiquity; Theophilus uses "saffron, with which silk is colored" over tin to imitate gold.
citation: Pliny, Natural History 21.17; Theophilus, De diversis artibus 1.32 (tr. Hendrie, 1847)
quote: Theophilus: "take saffron, with which silk is coloured, moistening it with clear of egg"; Nuruosmaniye: colours obtained "Yellow - Brown, Yellow, Bright yellow"; Pliny: "Saffron was already held in high esteem in the time of the Trojan War".
colour: Estimate from published colour descriptions (crocin gives a warm golden yellow on silk and wool, used to turn tin to gold); no measured swatch fetched. Saffron dyes yellow, not orange: it does not reach the orange gap.

name: Carbunculus
what: Pliny's carbunculus, the fiery red gem (the Alabandic kind cut at Alabanda: almandine garnet); the garnet of late antique cloisonne.
citation: Pliny, Natural History 37.25; The Met, ring with garnet, Roman (243672)
quote: Pliny: "In the first rank among these is carbunculus, so called from its resemblance to fire"; "the Alabandic stones ... are cut and polished at Alabanda"; Met 243672 medium: "Gold, carbuncle".
colour: Met 468366 primary image (DP30191), garnet cells: mean of pixels with sat>=0.45, hue 330-20, in the brighter half (50th-95th pct); the middle half reads 371213 and the Roman cabochon (Met 243672) 2C1A1F. The garnet-carbunculus equation is the usual reading, not stated by Pliny.

name: Coccum
what: Kermes (coccum, the "scarlet berry" of the holm oak, Kermes vermilio): the grain dye of Roman generals' cloaks.
citation: Pliny, Natural History 16.12, 21.22, 22.3
quote: Pliny 22.3: "the coccus, a dye reserved for the military costume of our generals"; 21.22: "the red, that of the kermes for instance, which, beginning in the tints of the rose, reflects ... the shades that are found in the Tyrian purple"; Nuruosmaniye: "Kermes with an alum mordant dyes wool and silk a bright red."
colour: Estimate from the descriptions (bright red leaning to crimson on alum-mordanted wool); no measured swatch fetched. Lighter than the deep-crimson gap.

name: Hysginum
what: Hysginum: cloth first dyed with kermes, then steeped in Tyrian purple; Vitruvius also dyes chalk with it to make purple paint.
citation: Pliny, Natural History 9.65, 35.26; Vitruvius, De architectura 7.14.1 (tr. Gwilt)
quote: Pliny 9.65: "to steep in Tyrian purple fabrics already dyed crimson with the berry of the kermes, in order to produce the hysginian tint"; Vitruvius: "Purple colours are also made by tinging chalk with madder-root and hysginum."
colour: Computed, not observed: crimson kermes red (Coccum A8202E) over-dyed toward the list's Tyrian Purple 4C1A3A, a deep purplish crimson.

name: Curalium
what: Red coral (Corallium rubrum), Pliny's curalium, prized from the Stoechades and Sicily; coral beads in Coptic necklaces of the 4th-7th c.
citation: Pliny, Natural History 32.11; The Met, Coptic beads (479605)
quote: Pliny: "its berries are white and soft while under water, but the moment they are removed from it, they become hard and red"; "from which last circumstance it is generally supposed to have received its name of “curalium.”"
colour: Met 479605 primary image (cop0489s1), the cluster of orange beads lower left: mean of pixels sat>=0.5, hue 10-35, brighter half (50th-95th pct; middle half D16F3A). That these are the coral in the mixed lot is my reading; the coral branches in Met 477066 are browner (8F4E22, weathered).

name: Glastum
what: Woad (Isatis tinctoria), Pliny's Gaulish glastum: the European indigo-blue dye; a light woad dye on wool is a greyish slate blue.
citation: Pliny, Natural History 22.2; BioColour Library, woad on wool
quote: Pliny: "There is a plant in Gaul, similar to the plantago in appearance, and known there by the name of “glastum:”"; BioColour Woad (5): Isatis tinctoria, natural white 100% wool, D65 "L* 48 a* -5 b* -15", sRGB 88 117 138.
colour: Measured: BioColour Library swatch Woad (5), CIELAB 48/-5/-15 (D65), sRGB 58758A as published.

name: Vitrum
what: Vitrum, the Latin name of woad (Greek isatis): the Britons' blue body dye in Caesar, and Vitruvius' dye for chalk to imitate indigo; a deep woad on wool.
citation: Vitruvius, De architectura 7.14.2; Caesar, Gallic War 5.14
quote: Vitruvius: "cretam selinusiam aut anulariam vitro, quod Graeci ισατιν appellant, inficientes, imitationem faciunt indici coloris"; Caesar: "Omnes vero se Britanni vitro inficiunt, quod caeruleum efficit colorem".
colour: Measured: BioColour Library swatch Woad (fresh leaves) (1) on wool yarn, CIELAB 21/-3/-9 (D65), sRGB 24343F as published; the Natural Indigo Finland woad pigment on wool reads 405D67.

name: Beryl
what: Beryl (aquamarine), which Pliny ranks best when it has "the pure green of the sea"; a Severan beryl intaglio.
citation: Pliny, Natural History 37.20; The Met, beryl intaglio of Julia Domna (251870)
quote: Pliny: "The most esteemed beryls are those which in colour resemble the pure green of the sea".
colour: Met 251870 primary image (h1_25.78.90): mean of stone pixels (hue 150-220, sat>=0.08) in the brighter half (50th-95th pct); the middle half reads 607A82. The photo shows a greyish sea-blue, not the pale mint of the gap.

name: Callaina
what: Pliny's callaina, a pale green stone "easily counterfeited in glass" (usually read as variscite/turquoise, callais); pale variscite beads on a Roman necklace.
citation: Pliny, Natural History 37.33; The Met, necklace with variscite beads (250988)
quote: Pliny: "the stone known as “callaina,” and of a pale green colour"; "There is no stone, too, that is more easily counterfeited in glass."
colour: Met 250988 original image (DP208005, 4000 px): median of a central patch on the pale bead upper right of a cropped detail (another bead reads B4B6A1). Callaina = variscite is a modern scholarly reading (Met names the beads variscite).

name: Conchyliatum
what: The "conchyliated" shellfish purple: the pale, highly esteemed tint got by dyeing with half-strength purple, shading through heliotrope and mallow.
citation: Pliny, Natural History 9.64, 21.22
quote: Pliny 9.64: "From this mixture a full colour is not obtained, but that pale tint, which is so highly esteemed; and the clearer it is, the less of it the wool has imbibed."; 21.22: "the tints of the heliotropium, and others of a deeper colour, the hues of the mallow".
colour: Estimate from the description: the list's Tyrian Purple 4C1A3A lightened and greyed toward a pale shellfish purple; no measured swatch fetched.
